items.stem: Lucas, a builder, agreed to install a new kitchen for Hana for $50 000, payable on completion. Lucas left after completing about half the work because of a better offer elsewhere. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: This is abandonment, so Lucas recovers nothing unless Hana freely accepted the part performance (Sumpter v Hedges). Reason: strict performance is required for entire contracts (Cutter v Powell; Re Moore & Landauer)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct outcome (this is abandonment, so Lucas recovers nothing unless Hana freely accepted the part performance (Sumpter v Hedges)). 1 mark: reason based on the rule, e.g. strict performance is required for entire contracts (Cutter v Powell; Re Moore & Landauer). [2]

items.stem: Omar, a builder, agreed to install a new kitchen for Ana for $50 000, payable on completion. Omar finished the work but it was so defective that much of it had to be redone at a cost of a third of the price. Advise Omar whether Omar can recover any payment from Ana.
items.answer: Law: strict performance is required for entire contracts (Cutter v Powell; Re Moore & Landauer); substantial performance: price less cost of defects (Hoenig v Isaacs) but not where defects are serious (Bolton v Mahadeva); acceptance of part performance must be free (Sumpter v Hedges); prevention allows quantum meruit (Planché v Colburn). Application: the contract was entire, payable on completion; Omar finished the work but it was so defective that much of it had to be redone at a cost of a third of the price; this is no substantial performance, so Omar may recover nothing (Bolton v Mahadeva). Conclusion: This is no substantial performance, so Omar may recover nothing (Bolton v Mahadeva).

AO2 Application [1]: applies the rules to the facts, e.g. the contract was entire, payable on completion; Omar finished the work but it was so defective that much of it had to be redone at a cost of a third of the price; this is no substantial performance, so Omar may recover nothing (Bolton v Mahadeva). items.stem: Explain three exceptions to the rule of strict performance.
items.answer: Divisible contracts (payment for each part); substantial performance (Hoenig v Isaacs); acceptance of partial performance (Sumpter v Hedges); prevention of performance by the other party (Planché v Colburn); valid tender of performance (Startup v Macdonald).

items.stem: Define the term 'frustration'.
items.answer: The automatic discharge of a contract where, after it is made and without the fault of either party, an event makes performance impossible, illegal or radically different from what was agreed.

items.stem: On 1 March Tariq agreed to work as a sound engineer for Mateo's concert promoter from 1 June. On 10 April Mateo told Tariq, "We will not need you after all." Advise Tariq on the options available.
items.answer: Law: anticipatory breach: a party indicates before performance is due that it will not perform (Hochster v De la Tour); the innocent party may accept the repudiation and sue at once, or affirm and wait; waiting risks the contract being frustrated (Avery v Bowden); performance after affirming requires a legitimate interest (White and Carter v McGregor); Tariq must mitigate loss by seeking other work. Application: Mateo's statement on 10 April is an anticipatory breach; Tariq can sue immediately without waiting for 1 June; Tariq should look for other work to mitigate. Conclusion: Tariq can accept the repudiation and claim damages immediately, subject to the duty to mitigate.

items.stem: Ines hired a riverside venue from Sipho for 15 June for a music festival, paying a deposit of $2 000 with the balance of $15 000 due on the day. A month before, the government banned all public gatherings in the area for the date. Advise Ines whether the contract has been discharged and whether the deposit can be recovered. Apply the relevant legal rules and case law to the facts, considering any alternative arguments.
items.answer: Law: frustration occurs where, without fault, performance becomes impossible, illegal or radically different (Taylor v Caldwell; Krell v Henry); increased cost or difficulty is not enough (Davis Contractors); self-induced events do not count (Maritime National Fish); LR(FC)A 1943 s1(2): money paid is recoverable and money due ceases to be payable, subject to the court allowing expenses. Application: the event means the contract is frustrated by supervening illegality; if frustrated, Ines can recover the $2 000 deposit and need not pay the $15 000, subject to a deduction for Sipho's expenses; if not frustrated, Ines's refusal is a breach. Conclusion: The contract is frustrated by supervening illegality.

items.stem: Kwame Ltd agreed to repair a bakery oven for Lina Ltd, a seafood exporter in Kathmandu, within three days. The repair took two weeks longer than agreed. items.answer: Lina Ltd can recover $6 000 in normal lost profits; the $75 000 special contract is too remote, as in Victoria Laundry. Reason: remoteness: losses arising naturally, or in the contemplation of both parties (Hadley v Baxendale)

items.stem: Elena Ltd agreed to repair a refrigeration unit for Aisha Ltd, a seafood exporter in Riyadh, within three days. The repair took three weeks longer than agreed. Aisha Ltd lost normal profits of $6 000 and also lost a special contract worth $40 000, which Elena Ltd had been told about when the contract was made. Advise Aisha Ltd on the damages it can recover from Elena Ltd. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: remoteness: losses arising naturally, or in the contemplation of both parties (Hadley v Baxendale); damages put the claimant in the position as if the contract had been performed (Robinson v Harman); unusual profits unknown to the defendant are too remote (Victoria Laundry); assumption of responsibility (The Achilleas); the claimant must mitigate. Application: the normal lost profits of $6 000 arise naturally from the delay (limb 1); the special contract worth $40 000 is recoverable under the second limb because Elena Ltd knew of it; Aisha Ltd should have tried to hire a replacement refrigeration unit to mitigate. Conclusion: Aisha Ltd can recover $6 000 in normal lost profits; the $40 000 special contract is recoverable under the second limb because Elena Ltd knew of it.

items.stem: Explain the difference between expectation and reliance damages.
items.answer: Expectation damages put the claimant in the position as if the contract had been performed (Robinson v Harman), e.g. loss of profit; reliance damages compensate wasted expenditure, putting the claimant back where they were (Anglia TV v Reed), used where profits are speculative.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Hoenig v Isaacs (1952) and Bolton v Mahadeva (1972).
items.answer: In Hoenig the defects were minor compared with the price, so there was substantial performance; in Bolton the defects were serious and costly, so there was no substantial performance and nothing was recoverable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each case; 1 mark contrast based on seriousness of defects. [3]

items.stem: Hana, a builder, agreed to install a new kitchen for Leila for $50 000, payable on completion. Hana finished the work, but there were minor defects costing about $800 to put right. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: This is substantial performance, so Hana can claim the price less $800 (Hoenig v Isaacs). Reason: strict performance is required for entire contracts (Cutter v Powell; Re Moore & Landauer)

items.stem: Tariq, a builder, agreed to build an extension for Mohammed for $50 000, payable on completion. Tariq was stopped halfway because Mohammed refused to let Tariq back on site. Advise Tariq whether Tariq can recover any payment from Mohammed. In your answer, refer to decided cases and assess how a court is likely to decide.
items.answer: Law: strict performance is required for entire contracts (Cutter v Powell; Re Moore & Landauer); substantial performance: price less cost of defects (Hoenig v Isaacs) but not where defects are serious (Bolton v Mahadeva); acceptance of part performance must be free (Sumpter v Hedges); prevention allows quantum meruit (Planché v Colburn). Application: the contract was entire, payable on completion; Tariq was stopped halfway because Mohammed refused to let Tariq back on site; this is prevention by Mohammed, so Tariq can claim a quantum meruit for work done (Planché v Colburn). Conclusion: This is prevention by Mohammed, so Tariq can claim a quantum meruit for work done (Planché v Colburn).

items.stem: Explain three situations in which a contract may be frustrated.
items.answer: Destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell); non-occurrence of the event that is the purpose of the contract (Krell v Henry); personal incapacity (Condor v Baron Knights); supervening illegality; government interference; long delay (Jackson v Union Marine).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per situation with case, up to 3. [3]

items.stem: Explain the effect of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943.
items.answer: Money paid before the frustrating event is recoverable and money due ceases to be payable (s1(2)); the court may allow the payee to retain or recover expenses; a party who has obtained a valuable benefit may have to pay a just sum (s1(3); BP v Hunt).
items.markingKey: 1 mark s1(2) recovery; 1 mark expenses; 1 mark s1(3) valuable benefit. [3]

items.answer: Frustration and the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943. Frustration occurs where, without fault, performance becomes impossible, illegal or radically different (Taylor v Caldwell; Krell v Henry).

items.stem: Ethan hired a hall in Auckland from Sipho for New Year's Eve for a company celebration, paying a deposit of $2 000 with the balance of $15 000 due on the day. Two days before, the venue was destroyed by fire without anyone's fault. Advise Ethan whether the contract has been discharged and whether the deposit can be recovered. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: frustration occurs where, without fault, performance becomes impossible, illegal or radically different (Taylor v Caldwell; Krell v Henry); increased cost or difficulty is not enough (Davis Contractors); self-induced events do not count (Maritime National Fish); LR(FC)A 1943 s1(2): money paid is recoverable and money due ceases to be payable, subject to the court allowing expenses. Application: the event means the contract is frustrated by destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell); if frustrated, Ethan can recover the $2 000 deposit and need not pay the $15 000, subject to a deduction for Sipho's expenses; if not frustrated, Ethan's refusal is a breach. Conclusion: The contract is frustrated by destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell).

Conclusion [1]: the contract is frustrated by destruction of the subject matter (Taylor v Caldwell) [3]

items.stem: On 1 March Mateo agreed to work as a chef for Kenji's travel company from 1 June. On 10 April Kenji told Mateo, "We will not need you after all." Advise Mateo on the options available. Explain the relevant law, apply it to the facts and evaluate the strength of any arguments available.
items.answer: Law: anticipatory breach: a party indicates before performance is due that it will not perform (Hochster v De la Tour); the innocent party may accept the repudiation and sue at once, or affirm and wait; waiting risks the contract being frustrated (Avery v Bowden); performance after affirming requires a legitimate interest (White and Carter v McGregor); Mateo must mitigate loss by seeking other work. Application: Kenji's statement on 10 April is an anticipatory breach; Mateo can sue immediately without waiting for 1 June; Mateo should look for other work to mitigate. Conclusion: Mateo can accept the repudiation and claim damages immediately, subject to the duty to mitigate.

items.stem: State what is meant by 'expectation loss'.
items.answer: Damages that put the claimant in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed (Robinson v Harman).

items.stem: Explain the duty to mitigate loss.
items.answer: The claimant must take reasonable steps to reduce the loss, e.g. buying substitute goods or seeking other work; loss that could have been avoided is not recoverable, but reasonable costs of mitigation are; the burden is on the defendant to show failure (British Westinghouse).
items.markingKey: 1 mark duty; 1 mark consequence; 1 mark example/case. [3]

items.stem: Nadia Ltd agreed to sell 20 laptops to Isla Ltd at $600 each, for delivery on 1 May. Nadia Ltd failed to deliver. On 1 May the market price was $780 each. Calculate the damages Isla Ltd can recover.
items.markingKey: Expectation damages = (market price − contract price) × quantity = ($780 − $600) × 20 = $3,600 [2]. [2]

items.stem: Explain when specific performance will not be granted.
items.answer: Where damages are adequate; for personal services; where constant supervision would be needed (Ryan; Co-op v Argyll); where the claimant has acted unfairly (clean hands) or delayed; where it would cause severe hardship; where there is no mutuality.

items.stem: Explain how injunctions can be used in contract law.
items.answer: A prohibitory injunction can restrain a breach of a negative stipulation, e.g. not to work for a competitor (Lumley v Wagner; Warner Bros v Nelson), but not if it would effectively compel performance of personal services (Page One Records v Britton).
items.markingKey: 1 mark prohibitory injunction; 1 mark negative stipulation case; 1 mark limitation. [3]

items.stem: Evaluate the extent to which the exceptions to strict performance make the law fair. Your answer should consider arguments on both sides and reach a conclusion.
items.answer: For: substantial performance prevents unjust enrichment; quantum meruit protects those prevented from performing; divisible contracts allow payment for parts. Against: strict rule still applies harshly (Cutter v Powell; Bolton v Mahadeva); acceptance must be free, which is hard where work is on land (Sumpter v Hedges); uncertainty over what is "substantial". Conclusion: The exceptions greatly reduce the harshness of the rule, though not completely.

items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, evaluate the doctrine of frustration.
items.answer: For: relieves parties from obligations made impossible by events beyond their control; narrow limits preserve the sanctity of contract (Davis Contractors); 1943 Act provides flexible financial adjustment. items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, evaluate the role of equitable remedies in contract law.
items.answer: For: provide justice where damages are inadequate (land, unique goods); flexible and discretionary; injunctions enforce negative promises. Against: discretion causes uncertainty; limits on personal services and supervision; cost and delay of seeking equitable relief. Conclusion: Equitable remedies fill important gaps, but their discretionary nature limits their reach.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge and understanding [4]: accurate explanation of the law with supporting authority, e.g. Beswick v Beswick (1967); Co-op v Argyll (1998); Lumley v Wagner (1852); Warner Bros v Nelson (1937); Page One Records v Britton (1968). AO3 Analysis and evaluation [6]: arguments supporting the view, e.g. provide justice where damages are inadequate (land, unique goods); flexible and discretionary; injunctions enforce negative promises; arguments against / problems, e.g. discretion causes uncertainty; limits on personal services and supervision; cost and delay of seeking equitable relief. Levels: L1 basic, descriptive points; L2 some accurate law with limited comment; L3 accurate law and some developed evaluation; L4 wide-ranging, accurate law with sustained, balanced evaluation and a reasoned conclusion.
